about: Sourced life stories for Paul's companions: Silas, Timothy, Titus, Luke, Apollos, Priscilla and Aquila. Written from Scripture and the reviewed dossier Research/People/church-pauls-circle.md.

silas-act-15-22.short: A leading man of the Jerusalem church and a prophet, who carried the council's letter to Antioch, then travelled with Paul and was jailed with him at Philippi.

paragraphs.text: Silas first appears in Jerusalem. The apostles and elders, with the whole church, chose him and Judas surnamed Barsabas, "chief men among the brethren", to go to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas. The two carried the council's letter to the Gentile believers and were to "tell you the same things by mouth". At Antioch, "being prophets also themselves", they exhorted the brethren with many words. Scripture names no family for Silas and does not say where he was born.

When Paul and Barnabas parted over John Mark, "Paul chose Silas", and they went through Syria and Cilicia, confirming the churches. At Derbe and Lystra Timothy joined them, and as they went through the cities they delivered the decrees of the apostles and elders at Jerusalem.

At Philippi he and Paul were drawn before the magistrates, beaten with many stripes, and made fast in the stocks. At midnight they "prayed, and sang praises unto God"; after an earthquake opened the doors, the jailor was baptized with all his house. Next day Paul would not be let out privily, because the magistrates had beaten them "being Romans", and the magistrates came and brought them out. They went to Lydia's house before they left the city.

At Thessalonica some believed and "consorted with Paul and Silas", until an uproar led the brethren to send the two away by night to Berea. When Paul was sent on to Athens, Silas and Timothy stayed at Berea; they were told to come "with all speed", and they reached Paul at Corinth, coming from Macedonia. That is the last time Acts names Silas.

Acts always calls him Silas. Paul's letters name a Silvanus beside Timothy: Christ was preached at Corinth "by me and Silvanus and Timotheus", and both letters to the Thessalonians open "Paul, and Silvanus, and Timotheus". 1 Peter was written "By Silvanus, a faithful brother". Scripture does not say whether Silvanus and Silas are one man, and it does not record where Silas went later or how he died.

timothy-act-16-1.short: A disciple Paul found at Derbe and Lystra, son of a believing Jewess and a Greek; Paul took him along and called him his own son in the faith.

paragraphs.text: When Paul came to Derbe and Lystra, "a certain disciple was there, named Timotheus", well reported of by the brethren at Lystra and Iconium. His mother was "a Jewess, and believed", and his father was a Greek. Paul writes that the "unfeigned faith" in Timothy dwelt first in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice, and that "from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures". Scripture does not give his father's name.

Paul wanted him to go with him, and circumcised him "because of the Jews which were in those quarters", for they all knew his father was a Greek. He went with Paul and Silas through the cities. He stayed with Silas at Berea and came on to Paul at Corinth, where, Paul writes, Christ was preached by Paul, Silvanus and Timotheus. 1 Thessalonians says Paul sent him from Athens to Thessalonica and that he came back with "good tidings of your faith and charity"; Acts does not mention him at Athens.

Paul sent him into Macedonia with Erastus while he himself stayed in Asia, and wrote to Corinth that he was sending "Timotheus, who is my beloved son, and faithful in the Lord": "Let no man therefore despise him". He was among those who went ahead of Paul to Troas. Paul names him beside himself at the head of 2 Corinthians, Philippians, Colossians, both letters to the Thessalonians and Philemon. To the Philippians Paul writes, "I have no man likeminded", and "as a son with the father, he hath served with me in the gospel".

Two letters are addressed to him. In the first, Paul says he had asked him "to abide still at Ephesus" when Paul went into Macedonia, tells him "Let no man despise thy youth", and reminds him of the gift given him "with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery". He also tells him to "use a little wine for thy stomach's sake and thine often infirmities".

In the second, Paul writes as a prisoner, remembers Timothy's tears, and asks him to come "shortly" and "before winter", bringing Mark and the cloak left at Troas. Scripture does not say whether he came. Hebrews tells its readers that "our brother Timothy is set at liberty"; it does not say from what, or whether this is the same Timothy. Scripture does not record his death.

titus-2co-2-13.short: A Greek believer whom Paul called his son and his partner; Paul sent him to Corinth, and left him in Crete to ordain elders in every city.

paragraphs.text: Titus is known only from Paul's letters; Acts never names him. Paul calls him "Titus my brother", "my partner and fellowhelper", and "mine own son after the common faith". He was a Greek. Scripture gives no home or family for him.

Paul took him up to Jerusalem with Barnabas, and writes that "neither Titus, who was with me, being a Greek, was compelled to be circumcised". Of the "false brethren" who came in to spy out their liberty, Paul says, "we gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour".

Paul came to Troas but "had no rest in my spirit, because I found not Titus my brother", and went on into Macedonia. There God "comforted us by the coming of Titus", who told Paul of the Corinthians' earnest desire and mourning, and whose spirit "was refreshed by you all".

Paul desired Titus to finish at Corinth the same grace he had begun there, and Titus went "of his own accord", with a brother "whose praise is in the gospel throughout all the churches" and another brother. Later in the same letter Paul asks the Corinthians, "Did Titus make a gain of you?"

The letter addressed to him says Paul left him in Crete "that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city". It asks him, when Artemas or Tychicus is sent to him, to come to Paul at Nicopolis, where Paul meant to winter, and to bring Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their journey. 2 Timothy says he had gone "unto Dalmatia". Scripture does not say whether he reached Nicopolis, or how his life ended.

luke-2co-13-13.short: A companion of Paul, called by him the beloved physician and a fellowlabourer; Scripture names him only three times, all in Paul's letters.

paragraphs.text: Scripture says very little about Luke: it names him three times, all in Paul's letters. In Colossians Paul sends greetings from "Luke, the beloved physician", and in Philemon he lists "Lucas" with Marcus, Aristarchus and Demas as "my fellowlabourers".
In 2 Timothy Paul writes as a prisoner, and says that Onesiphorus had sought him out in Rome. He tells Timothy that Demas, Crescens and Titus had gone, and "Only Luke is with me".

Scripture tells nothing else of him: not his home or family, not how he came to believe, and not his death. The third Gospel and Acts are both written to Theophilus, but neither names its writer; who wrote them is taken up on Luke's page.

apollos-act-18-24.short: A Jew born at Alexandria, eloquent and mighty in the scriptures, whom Priscilla and Aquila taught more perfectly; he worked at Corinth after Paul had planted.

paragraphs.text: Acts introduces him as "a certain Jew named Apollos, born at Alexandria, an eloquent man, and mighty in the scriptures", who came to Ephesus. He had been instructed in the way of the Lord, and "being fervent in the spirit" he taught diligently, "knowing only the baptism of John". Scripture does not say how he had first learned.

He began to speak boldly in the synagogue there. When Aquila and Priscilla heard him, they took him to them and "expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly". When he wished to go into Achaia, the brethren wrote to the disciples there to receive him; he "helped them much which had believed through grace", showing publicly by the scriptures "that Jesus was Christ".

He was at Corinth when Paul came to Ephesus. Paul's first letter to the Corinthians tells of believers there saying "I am of Paul; and I of Apollos", and Paul answers, "I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase". He says he has applied these things to himself and to Apollos so that none of them should be "puffed up for one against another".

Paul writes of "our brother Apollos" that he had greatly desired him to go to Corinth, "but his will was not at all to come at this time". The letter to Titus asks Titus to bring Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their journey, so that nothing should be wanting to them. Scripture says nothing more of him, and does not say that he wrote anything.

priscilla-act-18-2.short: Aquila's wife and fellow tentmaker, with whom Paul lodged at Corinth; with her husband she taught Apollos and kept a church in their house.

paragraphs.text: Priscilla was the wife of Aquila, a Jew born in Pontus. They had lately come from Italy, "because that Claudius had commanded all Jews to depart from Rome". At Corinth Paul came to them, and because he was of the same craft he stayed and worked with them, "for by their occupation they were tentmakers". Scripture names no children and does not say when they came to believe.

When Paul sailed for Syria, Priscilla and Aquila went with him as far as Ephesus, where he left them. There they heard Apollos speak boldly in the synagogue, took him to them, and "expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly".

Paul's letters send greetings from them and to them. Writing from Ephesus he says, "Aquila and Priscilla salute you much in the Lord, with the church that is in their house". In Romans he greets "Priscilla and Aquila my helpers in Christ Jesus", who "for my life laid down their own necks", and to whom all the churches of the Gentiles give thanks; he greets the church in their house as well. 2 Timothy sends a greeting to "Prisca and Aquila".

Scripture never names her without her husband, and in three of the six places where the KJV names them her name comes first. It does not say how they risked their necks for Paul, or how their lives ended.

aquila-act-18-2.short: A Jew born in Pontus, a tentmaker, and Priscilla's husband; Scripture always names the two together, and their story is told on their shared page.

paragraphs.text: Acts introduces him as "a certain Jew named Aquila, born in Pontus", lately come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had commanded all Jews to leave Rome. At Corinth Paul stayed and worked with them, for they were tentmakers and Paul was "of the same craft".

He and Priscilla sailed with Paul to Ephesus, where Paul left them, and there the two of them took Apollos to them and taught him the way of God more perfectly. Paul, writing from Ephesus, sends greetings from "Aquila and Priscilla" and "the church that is in their house".

Paul calls the two of them "my helpers in Christ Jesus", who had laid down their own necks for his life, and 2 Timothy sends a greeting to "Prisca and Aquila". Scripture never names him without his wife, names no children, and does not record his death. Their life together is told more fully on the page for Priscilla and Aquila.
